# Model-based meta-analysis {#sec-mbma}

```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
#| cache: false
source(if (file.exists("_common.R")) "_common.R" else "chapters/_common.R")
```

## Where you are

A model-based meta-analysis (MBMA) fits a dose-response and time-course model to published summary data: one mean per study arm and visit, with its standard error and the number of patients behind it. There are no individual patients. Each row counts according to its precision, and arms differ from one another more than their sampling error alone explains.

This chapter fits the bundled `mbma_placebo` example. It covers the arm-level data shape and `ferx_mbma_data()`, inverse-variance weighting with `weight =` on the error model, between-arm variability as a weighted kappa, an unstructured placebo time course as a theta level block, and how to read, save and resample such a fit. If your meta-analysis already exists as a compartment-free nlmixr2 model, `ferxtranslate::nlmixr2_to_ferx()` from the [ferxtranslate](https://github.com/FeRx-NLME/translator) package translates it to a ferx model to start from (`output =` writes the file).

::: {.callout-important}
## Needs ferx-r newer than {{< var ferx_r_release >}}
This chapter needs the build the book is pinned to (@sec-installation). ferx-r {{< var ferx_r_release >}} has no `ferx_mbma_data()` (nor `print()` for its result), no `mbma_placebo` example, no `fit$theta_levels` and no `ferx_contrast_vpc()` (nor `print()` or `plot()` for its result). Fitting a data.frame, the `.fitrx` round trip of a level block, the standard error and SIR interval of each level, `ferx_sir()` / `ferx_covariance()` following the fit's own settings, the fit's verdict (`fit$status`, `fit$status_label`, `fit$status_reasons`) and `fit$held_at_bound`, a profiled level block (`profile`, `fit$profiled_blocks`, bounds on it and the deprecated `fit$profiled_levels_at_bound`), a level block read by a `[binary_model]` predictor (and profiled there), the probit link of `[binary_model]`, `pnorm()` in a model expression, nested variability levels (`level`, `fit$kappa_levels`, `fit$ebe_kappas_by_level`, the `nested_levels` example) and a within-arm residual `correlation` line are newer than {{< var ferx_r_release >}} as well.
:::

::: {.callout-warning}
## Maturity: beta
At the pinned engine, ferx-core labels the MBMA features this chapter uses **beta** ([feature maturity at this build](26-reference.qmd#sec-reference-maturity)): [theta level blocks](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/parameters.html#theta-level-blocks), [profiled level blocks](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/parameters.html#profiled-level-blocks), [nested levels](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/iov.html#nested-levels), the within-arm residual [`correlation`](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/residual-correlation.html) line, `weight =` on the error model ([residual weighting](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/error-model.html#residual-weighting-weight-...)) and on a kappa ([sample-size-weighted IOV](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/iov.html#sample-size-weighted-iov-weight-...)), and [compartment-free models](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/structural-model.html#compartment-free-models-the-pred-equivalent) such as `mbma_placebo`. `[binary_model]` and `pnorm()`, used in the responder and proportion sections, carry no maturity label at this build. The ferx-core [feature maturity](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/maturity.html) page follows the newest engine and may be ahead of the pin.
:::

## The data

```{r}
#| label: packages
#| message: false
library(ferx)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
```

The bundled data are synthetic: six studies of a symptom score (lower is better), each with a placebo arm and two or three dose arms, observed at week 0 and three later visits. Each row is one arm at one visit:

```{r}
#| label: data
mbma <- ferx_example("mbma_placebo")
mbma_dir <- file.path(tempdir(), "mbma")
dir.create(mbma_dir, showWarnings = FALSE)
arm_data <- read.csv(mbma$data)
head(arm_data, 5)
arm_data |>
  group_by(STUDY) |>
  summarise(arms = n_distinct(OCC), weeks = paste(sort(unique(TIME)), collapse = ", "),
            doses = paste(sort(unique(DOSE)), collapse = ", "),
            min_NARM = min(NARM), max_NARM = max(NARM))
```

The columns follow one convention:

- `ID` and `STUDY` are the study. A random effect on `ID` is therefore between-study variability.
- `OCC` is the arm within the study, numbered from 1. A kappa, the random effect that is drawn once per occasion, is therefore between-arm variability.
- `DV` is the reported arm mean, `SE` its standard error and `NARM` the number of patients in the arm. `DOSE` is the arm's dose; placebo arms have 0.
- There are no dose records. The model is compartment-free: `DOSE` is a covariate, not an amount.

### Building the dataset with `ferx_mbma_data()`

Published summaries rarely come in this layout. `ferx_mbma_data()` turns a table with one row per study, arm and timepoint into it, and checks it on the way. The script that generated the bundled data ends with that call, so running it gives both the raw table (`arms`) and the bundled file:

```{r}
#| label: generator
generator <- system.file("examples", "mbma_placebo", "simulate_dataset.R", package = "ferx")
gen <- new.env()
gen$mbma_out_csv <- file.path(mbma_dir, "rebuilt.csv")
sys.source(generator, envir = gen)
head(gen$arms, 5)
```

The raw table names its columns as a publication would: a trial label, an arm number, the week, the arm mean, the between-patient standard deviation and the arm size. `ferx_mbma_data()` takes the name of each:

```{r}
#| label: mbma-data
arm_table <- ferx_mbma_data(gen$arms, study = "trial", arm = "arm", time = "week",
                            mean = "mean", sd = "sd", n = "n", covariates = "DOSE")
arm_table
attr(arm_table, "arms") |> head(4)
all.equal(read.csv(gen$mbma_out_csv), arm_data)
```

`print()` on a `ferx_mbma_data` object reports the number of studies and arms and the range of `SE * sqrt(NARM)`, the between-patient SD the standard errors imply. That range is a quick check that the precision column holds what you think it does. The `arms` attribute maps each `(STUDY, OCC)` back to the original trial and arm labels, and the rebuilt file equals the bundled one.

The arguments:

- `data` is the arm table. `study`, `arm`, `time`, `mean` and `n` name its columns.
- Give exactly one of `se` (the standard error of the arm mean) or `sd` (the between-patient SD, converted to `sd / sqrt(n)`, as the message above says).
- `scale` is `"continuous"` (the default), `"proportion"` or `"percent"`. The last two check the range of `mean`, and `"percent"` divides `mean` and `se` by 100.
- `covariates` carries further columns through. Character and factor columns are coded as integers, with the codes in `attr(d, "codes")`.
- `levels` adds a `LEVEL_IDX` column that numbers the observed combinations of the named columns, for a counted level block `theta NAME[N]`. `index` takes your own numbering instead, for example to pool visits into windows. This chapter's model uses the data-driven form, which needs neither.

```{r}
#| label: mbma-levels
with_index <- ferx_mbma_data(gen$arms, study = "trial", arm = "arm", time = "week",
                             mean = "mean", sd = "sd", n = "n", levels = c("STUDY", "TIME"))
head(attr(with_index, "levels"), 5)
```

The checks catch preparation mistakes that would otherwise fit without complaint. A score read as a proportion is refused, and a study left with one arm is flagged, because nothing within it informs the treatment effect:

```{r}
#| label: mbma-data-checks
try(ferx_mbma_data(gen$arms, study = "trial", arm = "arm", time = "week",
                   mean = "mean", sd = "sd", n = "n", scale = "proportion"))
one_arm <- subset(gen$arms, !(trial == "T01" & arm > 1))
invisible(ferx_mbma_data(one_arm, study = "trial", arm = "arm", time = "week",
                         mean = "mean", sd = "sd", n = "n"))
```

The result goes straight into the fitting functions: their `data` argument takes a data.frame as well as a CSV path (shown below).

## Minimal runnable call

The model has four parts: a typical placebo level `TVE0` with a between-study random effect `ETA_E0`, a placebo time course `PLACEBO` with one level per study and visit, an Emax dose-response that builds up over time, and a between-arm random effect `KAPPA_ARM`:

```{r}
#| label: model
invisible(ferx_model_get_section(mbma$model, "parameters"))
invisible(ferx_model_get_section(mbma$model, "individual_parameters"))
invisible(ferx_model_get_section(mbma$model, "structural_model"))
invisible(ferx_model_get_section(mbma$model, "error_model"))
invisible(ferx_model_get_section(mbma$model, "fit_options"))
```

```{r}
#| label: check-arms
#| include: false
# The paragraph below counts the arms and says each study has one placebo arm.
arms_all <- distinct(arm_data, STUDY, OCC, DOSE)
stopifnot(sum(arms_all$DOSE == 0) == n_distinct(arm_data$STUDY),
          all(tapply(arms_all$DOSE == 0, arms_all$STUDY, sum) == 1), sum(arms_all$DOSE > 0) > 0)
```

Placebo and treated arms are fitted together, in one likelihood: all `r nrow(arms_all)` arms of the `r n_distinct(arm_data$STUDY)` studies, `r sum(arms_all$DOSE == 0)` on placebo and `r sum(arms_all$DOSE > 0)` on an active dose. Every arm of a study shares that study's placebo levels, and the Emax term, which is zero at `DOSE = 0`, adds the drug effect on top. The model therefore assumes that the placebo response is the same in a study's placebo and treated arms and adds to the drug effect. Within a study, the difference between a treated arm and its placebo arm is what identifies `EMAX`, `ED50` and `ET50`.

`iov_column = OCC` makes each arm an occasion. The fit is quick:

```{r}
#| label: fit
fit <- ferx_fit(mbma$model, mbma$data, verbose = FALSE)
fit
```

```{r}
#| label: check-fit
#| include: false
# The prose below says the fit converged, has 18 free placebo levels (fewer than
# the 20 at which print() collapses a block) and a computed covariance step.
stopifnot(isTRUE(fit$converged), fit$covariance_status == "computed",
          sum(!is.na(fit$theta_levels$theta_name)) == 18)
```

The fit converges and the covariance step runs. `fit$converged` is about the optimizer: it stopped normally and, for a fit like this one, at a stationary point (@sec-fit-verdict says when that is tested). Whether the fit can be used as it stands is `fit$status`, which also takes in the covariance step, the critical warnings and the evaluation budget; `fit$status_label` spells it as the `STATUS` line of the print does, and `fit$status_reasons` lists what stands in the way:

```{r}
#| label: status
fit[c("converged", "status", "status_label", "status_reasons")]
fit$held_at_bound
```

```{r}
#| label: check-status
#| include: false
# The prose: the first fit is CONVERGED with no reasons and no parameter held.
stopifnot(identical(fit$status, "converged"), identical(fit$status_label, "CONVERGED"),
          length(fit$status_reasons) == 0, is.data.frame(fit$held_at_bound), nrow(fit$held_at_bound) == 0)
```

This fit is `r fit$status_label`, with no reasons. `fit$held_at_bound` lists every parameter the covariance step gives no standard error for, such as a variance collapsed onto its lower guard or a profiled level on its bound; none is here. Read the status, its reasons and `held_at_bound` before trusting an MBMA fit. With few studies a variance can collapse, and a covariance step can fail, while `converged` stays `TRUE`: both happen later in this chapter (*Nested levels* and *Uncertainty*).

The `ferx_mbma_data()` table fits the same way, with no file in between:

```{r}
#| label: fit-table
fit_table <- ferx_fit(mbma$model, arm_table, verbose = FALSE)
c(file = fit$ofv, table = fit_table$ofv)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-fit-table
#| include: false
# The prose: the same fit to the printed digits, not bit-identical.
stopifnot(abs(fit_table$ofv - fit$ofv) < 1e-4, isTRUE(all.equal(fit_table$theta, fit$theta, tolerance = 1e-4)))
```

The two agree to the printed digits but are not bit-identical: the bundled file stores each standard error to 15 significant digits, while `arm_table` holds them at full precision. The rest of this chapter reads the fit of the file one part at a time.

## Reading the result

### Residual weighting: `weight =` on the error model

The error model is `DV ~ additive(ADD_ERR) weight = SE`, with `ADD_ERR` fixed at a variance of 1. `weight = W` multiplies the additive residual SD by `W`, so each row's residual SD is its own reported standard error, and the row counts `1 / SE^2` in the objective. This is inverse-variance weighting. The weight is a property of the data row, so it may use covariates, `TIME` and thetas, but not random effects or predictions.

`DV`, `PRED`, `IPRED` and simulations all stay on the natural scale, so nothing has to be transformed back before plotting. The individual weighted residual is the residual divided by that row's standard error:

```{r}
#| label: weighted-residual
head(fit$sdtab[, c("ID", "TIME", "DV", "IPRED", "IWRES")], 4)
all.equal(fit$sdtab$IWRES, (arm_data$DV - fit$sdtab$IPRED) / arm_data$SE)
```

Keep `sigma` fixed at 1 when the weights are the reported standard errors of a continuous endpoint: the weight already carries the whole precision, and a free sigma would count the scale twice. The ferx-core [error model](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/error-model.html#residual-weighting-weight-...) page describes the other convention, a free sigma for a weighted logit of a responder proportion.

### Between-arm variability: the weighted kappa

Two arms of the same study at the same dose would still not give the same mean: arms differ by more than their standard errors. That between-treatment-arm variability is smaller for a larger arm. The model declares it on the kappa:

```
kappa KAPPA_ARM ~ 4.0 (sd) weight = NARM
```

`weight = NARM` means the kappa of an arm with `NARM` patients is drawn from a normal distribution with variance γ² / `NARM`. ferx estimates γ², the variance for an arm of one patient, which is the quantity a published MBMA reports. Printed on its own, its SD looks large, so the fit prints the SD at the typical arm beside it, on the line that starts `weight = NARM`. The same numbers are in the fit:

```{r}
#| label: kappa
gamma2 <- fit$omega_iov["KAPPA_ARM", "KAPPA_ARM"]
c(gamma2 = gamma2, se = unname(fit$se_kappa["KAPPA_ARM"]))
fit$kappa_weights
fit$kappa_weight_typical
fit$kappa_param_types
```

```{r}
#| label: kappa-report
arm_sizes <- distinct(arm_data, STUDY, OCC, NARM)$NARM
data.frame(
  arm = c("one patient", "smallest arm", "typical arm (ferx)", "largest arm"),
  NARM = c(1, min(arm_sizes), fit$kappa_weight_typical, max(arm_sizes))
) |>
  mutate(between_arm_sd = sqrt(gamma2 / NARM))
```

```{r}
#| label: check-kappa-report
#| include: false
# The prose reports gamma^2 as the estimate, compares it with the generator's
# GAMMA2 through its 95% interval, and contrasts the typical arm with median().
lo <- gamma2 - 1.96 * fit$se_kappa[["KAPPA_ARM"]]
hi <- gamma2 + 1.96 * fit$se_kappa[["KAPPA_ARM"]]
stopifnot(gen$GAMMA2 > lo, gen$GAMMA2 < hi,
          fit$kappa_weight_typical %in% arm_sizes,
          median(arm_sizes) != fit$kappa_weight_typical)
```

So the convention for a report is: give the estimate as the unweighted γ² (`r signif(gamma2, 4)`, standard error `r signif(fit$se_kappa[["KAPPA_ARM"]], 3)`), and print beside it the effective between-arm SD at the median arm, `r sprintf("%.2f", sqrt(gamma2 / fit$kappa_weight_typical))` score points at `NARM` = `r fit$kappa_weight_typical`. The generator used γ² = `r gen$GAMMA2`, inside the estimate's 95% interval. With `r length(arm_sizes)` arms the median falls between two arm sizes. R's `median()` averages them (`r median(arm_sizes)`), while ferx takes an observed arm size, so read the typical arm from `fit$kappa_weight_typical` rather than recomputing it.

`KAPPA_ARM` enters `BASE` additively, so `fit$kappa_param_types` is `additive`, and the print shows an SD rather than a CV%. The kappa's shrinkage, `fit$shrinkage_kappa`, is a fraction (`r round(fit$shrinkage_kappa, 3)`), not a percentage.

### TVE0 is each study's mean placebo level

`PLACEBO[STUDY, TIME]` gives every study and visit its own placebo level, so no parametric placebo curve can bias the drug effect. Together with `TVE0` and the study random effect `ETA_E0`, those levels have one degree of freedom too many per study: a study's level could move up and its `ETA_E0` down by the same amount. The block's `contrast = sum_to_zero_within` removes it by making each study's levels sum to zero.

That convention changes what `TVE0` means. `TVE0 + ETA_E0` is a study's mean placebo level over its own visits, not its week-0 value, and the placebo levels are deviations from that mean. In this example the placebo score improves over time, so a study's week-0 placebo level tends to lie above its mean:

```{r}
#| label: tve0
levels_fit <- fit$theta_levels
cells <- distinct(arm_data, STUDY, TIME) |>
  arrange(STUDY, TIME) |>
  mutate(label = paste0("STUDY=", STUDY, ",TIME=", TIME))
stopifnot(identical(cells$label, levels_fit$label))
cells$placebo_level <- levels_fit$value
study_means <- data.frame(STUDY = as.integer(fit$ebe_etas$ID), ETA_E0 = fit$ebe_etas$ETA_E0) |>
  mutate(mean_placebo = fit$theta[["TVE0"]] + ETA_E0)
cells |>
  filter(TIME == 0) |>
  left_join(study_means, by = "STUDY") |>
  transmute(STUDY, mean_placebo, week0_placebo = mean_placebo + placebo_level)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-tve0
#| include: false
# The prose counts the studies whose week-0 level lies above the study mean
# ("tends to" needs a majority), and says the realised mean placebo level, not
# the nominal 50, is inside TVE0's interval and closer to the estimate.
week0 <- cells$placebo_level[cells$TIME == 0]
tve0 <- fit$theta[["TVE0"]]; tve0_se <- fit$se_theta[["TVE0"]]
stopifnot(sum(week0 > 0) > length(week0) / 2,
          abs(tve0 - gen$tve0_realised) < 1.96 * tve0_se,
          abs(tve0 - gen$TVE0) > abs(tve0 - gen$tve0_realised))
```

In `r sum(week0 > 0)` of the `r length(week0)` studies the week-0 level is above the study's mean`r if (any(week0 <= 0)) sprintf("; in study %s it is %s below it", paste(cells$STUDY[cells$TIME == 0][week0 <= 0], collapse = " and "), paste(round(-week0[week0 <= 0], 2), collapse = " and ")) else ""`. Reporting `TVE0` as "the baseline" would therefore typically understate the week-0 level.

The generator's nominal week-0 level is `r gen$TVE0`, but that is not what `TVE0` estimates. The truth to compare with is the realised mean placebo level over the six studies, `r round(gen$tve0_realised, 2)`, which the generator printed above. The estimate, `r round(fit$theta[["TVE0"]], 2)` (standard error `r round(fit$se_theta[["TVE0"]], 2)`), is close to it. The drug parameters are estimated with the generator's values inside their 95% intervals:

```{r}
#| label: drug-truth
truth <- c(TVE0 = gen$tve0_realised, EMAX = gen$EMAX, ED50 = gen$ED50, ET50 = gen$ET50)
data.frame(truth = truth, estimate = fit$theta[names(truth)],
           lower95 = fit$theta[names(truth)] - 1.96 * fit$se_theta[names(truth)],
           upper95 = fit$theta[names(truth)] + 1.96 * fit$se_theta[names(truth)])
```

```{r}
#| label: check-drug-truth
#| include: false
# "the generator's values inside their 95% intervals"
est <- fit$theta[names(truth)]; se <- fit$se_theta[names(truth)]
stopifnot(all(truth > est - 1.96 * se), all(truth < est + 1.96 * se))
```

### The placebo levels: `fit$theta_levels`

`fit$theta_levels` has one row per level of every level block. The 24 study-by-visit cells here give 24 rows. Under `sum_to_zero_within`, one level per study is not estimated but derived as minus the sum of the others, so it has no theta of its own: its `theta_name` is `NA`. The `value` column holds the fitted value of every level, derived ones included, so each study's values sum to zero. `se` is each level's standard error: a free level's own, and for a derived level the delta-method standard error of the negated sum. (`sir_lo` and `sir_hi` stay empty until SIR runs, below.)

```{r}
#| label: theta-levels
head(levels_fit, 5)
sum(is.na(levels_fit$theta_name))
round(tapply(levels_fit$value, levels_fit$group, sum), 10)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-theta-levels
#| include: false
stopifnot(nrow(levels_fit) == 24, sum(is.na(levels_fit$theta_name)) == 6,
          all(abs(tapply(levels_fit$value, levels_fit$group, sum)) < 1e-8),
          all(is.finite(levels_fit$se) & levels_fit$se > 0), all(is.na(levels_fit$sir_lo)))
```

Because `value` and `se` are complete, the placebo time course and its uncertainty plot straight from them. The level labels come in the order of the sorted `(STUDY, TIME)` cells, which the `stopifnot()` in the `tve0` chunk confirmed, so `cells` already carries each level's study and visit:

```{r}
#| label: fig-placebo-levels
#| fig-cap: "Fitted placebo levels with 95% intervals from their standard errors: each study's deviation from its own mean placebo level, by visit. Every study's levels sum to zero."
cells$se <- levels_fit$se
ggplot(cells, aes(TIME, placebo_level, colour = factor(STUDY))) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, colour = "grey60") +
  geom_line() +
  geom_pointrange(aes(ymin = placebo_level - 1.96 * se, ymax = placebo_level + 1.96 * se),
                  position = position_dodge(width = 0.6), size = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Week", y = "Placebo level (score points)", colour = "Study")
```

### A large level block prints compactly

A real MBMA can have hundreds of study-by-visit cells. `print()` moves a level block with 20 or more free coefficients into a one-line THETA BLOCKS summary (count, minimum, median, maximum), so the structural parameters stay readable. This model has 18, so its print above lists them all.

A model with study as a fixed effect has more. Dropping `ETA_E0` and switching to `contrast = sum_to_zero` over all levels leaves 23 free levels, and `TVE0` becomes the mean of all 24 cells:

```{r}
#| label: fixed-study
fixed_lines <- readLines(mbma$model)
fixed_lines <- fixed_lines[!grepl("omega ETA_E0", fixed_lines)]
fixed_lines <- sub("BASE = TVE0 + PLACEBO + ETA_E0 + KAPPA_ARM", "BASE = TVE0 + PLACEBO + KAPPA_ARM",
                   fixed_lines, fixed = TRUE)
fixed_lines <- sub("contrast = sum_to_zero_within", "contrast = sum_to_zero", fixed_lines, fixed = TRUE)
# Stop unless all three edits were made: no ETA_E0 left outside comments, and the new contrast in place.
stopifnot(!any(grepl("^[^#]*ETA_E0", fixed_lines)), any(grepl("contrast = sum_to_zero]", fixed_lines, fixed = TRUE)))
fixed_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_fixed_study.ferx")
writeLines(fixed_lines, fixed_model)
invisible(ferx_model_get_section(fixed_model, "individual_parameters"))
fit_fixed <- ferx_fit(fixed_model, mbma$data, verbose = FALSE)
fit_fixed
```

```{r}
#| label: check-fixed-study
#| include: false
# The prose: 23 free levels shown as one THETA BLOCKS line; every level still in
# fit$theta; the structure line names the block once.
printed <- capture.output(print(fit_fixed))
structure_line <- grep("^  Structural:", printed, value = TRUE)
stopifnot(isTRUE(fit_fixed$converged), any(grepl("THETA BLOCKS", printed)),
          sum(!is.na(fit_fixed$theta_levels$theta_name)) == 23,
          sum(grepl("^PLACEBO\\[", names(fit_fixed$theta))) == 23,
          grepl("PLACEBO[STUDY, TIME] (23 coefficients)", structure_line, fixed = TRUE),
          !grepl("PLACEBO[STUDY=", structure_line, fixed = TRUE))
```

The THETA table now shows the four structural parameters and one line for `PLACEBO`, and the `Structural:` line under MODEL STRUCTURE names the block once with its number of coefficients, whatever its size. Every coefficient is still in `fit_fixed$theta`, and `fit_fixed$theta_levels` still has every level with its value.

The study random effect and the fixed study levels are two ways to carry between-study differences. This chapter does not compare them: with six studies the choice rests on what the analysis needs, not on one fit statistic.

### Profiling a large level block

A level block that the prediction reads linearly, as `BASE` reads `PLACEBO` here, can be declared `profile`. So can one read inside a single logit or probit link that is the whole prediction, such as an observed proportion `y = inv_logit(TVL + PLACEBO + ...)` or `y = pnorm(...)` (see [An observed proportion](#sec-mbma-proportion) below, and [through a link](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/parameters.html#through-a-link) in ferx-core). So can one read by the `logit` or `probit` predictor of a `[binary_model]`, whose link is implicit (see [A responder endpoint](#sec-mbma-responder) below). FOCE and FOCEI then solve its levels exactly at every outer step, so the optimizer searches only the other parameters. It is meant for placebo models with hundreds of cells, too many for the optimizer to search. The declaration keeps its bounds and only adds the word:

```{r}
#| label: profile
profiled_lines <- sub("contrast = sum_to_zero](0.0, -50.0, 50.0)",
                      "contrast = sum_to_zero](0.0, -50.0, 50.0) profile", fixed_lines, fixed = TRUE)
stopifnot(any(grepl("contrast = sum_to_zero](0.0, -50.0, 50.0) profile", profiled_lines, fixed = TRUE)))
profiled_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_fixed_study_profiled.ferx")
writeLines(profiled_lines, profiled_model)
fit_profiled <- ferx_fit(profiled_model, mbma$data, verbose = FALSE)
fit_profiled$profiled_blocks
data.frame(levels = c("estimated", "profiled"),
           ofv = c(fit_fixed$ofv, fit_profiled$ofv),
           n_parameters = c(fit_fixed$n_parameters, fit_profiled$n_parameters),
           seconds = round(c(fit_fixed$wall_time_secs, fit_profiled$wall_time_secs), 2))
rbind(estimated = fit_fixed$theta[1:4], profiled = fit_profiled$theta[1:4])
grep("profiled", capture.output(print(fit_profiled)), value = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-profile
#| include: false
# The prose: the same objective (to the optimizer's tolerance) and parameter count, the
# structural estimates within a small fraction of their standard errors, slower on this small
# block (only the direction is checked: the ratio itself moves with machine load), every level
# flagged profiled.
structural <- names(fit_fixed$theta)[1:4]
stopifnot(isTRUE(fit_profiled$converged), identical(fit_profiled$profiled_blocks, "PLACEBO"),
          abs(fit_profiled$ofv - fit_fixed$ofv) < 1e-3,
          fit_profiled$n_parameters == fit_fixed$n_parameters,
          all(abs(fit_profiled$theta[structural] - fit_fixed$theta[structural]) < 0.1 * fit_fixed$se_theta[structural]),
          fit_profiled$wall_time_secs > fit_fixed$wall_time_secs,
          all(fit_profiled$theta_levels$profiled), !any(fit_fixed$theta_levels$profiled),
          sum(grepl("^PLACEBO\\[", names(fit_profiled$theta))) == 23,
          length(fit_profiled$profiled_levels_at_bound) == 0)
# The scope paragraph: Laplace (one node or adaptive quadrature) is accepted, and a method other
# than FOCE / FOCEI / Laplace is refused with E_PROFILE_SCOPE.
profile_scope_code <- function(method, settings = list()) tryCatch({
  suppressWarnings(ferx_fit(profiled_model, mbma$data, method = method,
                            settings = c(list(maxiter = 0), settings), verbose = FALSE)); "fitted"
}, error = function(e) e$code)
stopifnot(identical(profile_scope_code("saem"), "E_PROFILE_SCOPE"),
          identical(profile_scope_code("laplace"), "fitted"),
          identical(profile_scope_code("laplace", list(n_agq = 3)), "fitted"))
```

The profiled fit reaches the same objective, to the optimizer's tolerance (less than `r format(10^ceiling(log10(abs(fit_profiled$ofv - fit_fixed$ofv) + 1e-15)), scientific = TRUE)` OFV units apart), and structural estimates that differ by a small fraction of their standard errors. It is not faster here: with 23 levels it took `r sprintf("%.1f", fit_profiled$wall_time_secs / fit_fixed$wall_time_secs)` times as long when this page was rendered (the ratio varies with the machine and its load). Profile a block when it is too large to search, not to speed up a small one. Nothing about the model changes. The levels stay in `fit_profiled$theta` and in `theta_levels`, whose `profiled` column marks them, and they count in `n_parameters` and BIC, so a likelihood-ratio test against an unprofiled model is valid.

All three covariance methods are accepted on a profiled fit. `ferx_covariance()` without `covariance_method` repeats the fit's own, which `fit$covariance_method` records:

```{r}
#| label: profile-covariance
fit_profiled$covariance_method
profiled_s <- ferx_covariance(fit_profiled, covariance_method = "s")
profiled_s$covariance_status
profiled_rsr <- ferx_covariance(fit_profiled, covariance_method = "rsr")
data.frame(r = fit_profiled$se_theta[1:4], rsr = profiled_rsr$se_theta[1:4])
summary(profiled_rsr$theta_levels$se / fit_profiled$theta_levels$se)
rsr_note <- grep("W_COV_RSR_ONE_SUBJECT_LEVELS", profiled_rsr$warnings, value = TRUE, fixed = TRUE)
cat(strwrap(rsr_note, 90)[1:2], sep = "\n")
```

```{r}
#| label: check-profile-covariance
#| include: false
# The prose: the fit's own method is r; s fails on the score cross-product; rsr runs, warns that
# every level is read by one subject, and gives every level a smaller SE than r.
rsr_warnings <- ferx_get_warnings(profiled_rsr, as_df = TRUE)
stopifnot(identical(fit_profiled$covariance_method, "r"), profiled_s$covariance_status == "failed",
          any(grepl("rank-deficient", ferx_get_warnings(profiled_s, as_df = TRUE)$message)),
          profiled_rsr$covariance_status == "computed",
          any(rsr_warnings$category == "covariance_step" & grepl("W_COV_RSR_ONE_SUBJECT_LEVELS", rsr_warnings$message, fixed = TRUE)),
          all(profiled_rsr$theta_levels$se < fit_profiled$theta_levels$se))
```

`"s"` fails for the reason the uncertainty section below explains: six studies cannot determine `r fit_profiled$n_parameters` parameters. `"rsr"` runs, but each level of this block is read by a single study, and at the estimate such a level's own score is nearly zero. The sandwich then carries almost none of the level's own variability: every level's `rsr` standard error is smaller than its `r` one, at `r sprintf("%.2f", min(profiled_rsr$theta_levels$se / fit_profiled$theta_levels$se))` to `r sprintf("%.2f", max(profiled_rsr$theta_levels$se / fit_profiled$theta_levels$se))` times its size, and ferx says so in a `covariance_step` warning (`W_COV_RSR_ONE_SUBJECT_LEVELS`). Read the level standard errors from `"r"`.

#### Bounds on a profiled block

The bounds of a profiled block work as they do for an estimated one: the levels are then the exact minimiser over that box. The box above, −50 to 50, is far from every level. Tighten its upper bound to 5, which one level exceeds:

```{r}
#| label: profile-bounds
tight_lines <- sub("contrast = sum_to_zero](0.0, -50.0, 50.0) profile",
                   "contrast = sum_to_zero](0.0, -50.0, 5.0) profile", profiled_lines, fixed = TRUE)
stopifnot(any(grepl("contrast = sum_to_zero](0.0, -50.0, 5.0) profile", tight_lines, fixed = TRUE)))
tight_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_fixed_study_profiled_tight.ferx")
writeLines(tight_lines, tight_model)
fit_tight <- ferx_fit(tight_model, mbma$data, verbose = FALSE)
fit_tight$held_at_bound
held <- fit_tight$held_at_bound$parameter
c(unbounded = fit_profiled$theta[[held]], bounded = fit_tight$theta[[held]])
c(unbounded = fit_profiled$ofv, bounded = fit_tight$ofv)
subset(fit_tight$theta_levels, theta_name %in% held, c(label, value, se))
subset(ferx_get_warnings(fit_tight, as_df = TRUE), category == "boundary_estimate")$message
```

```{r}
#| label: check-profile-bounds
#| include: false
# The prose: one level held on the upper bound, which it exceeds unbounded; the objective rises;
# its SE is NA in theta_levels; a boundary_estimate warning; every other level
# keeps a standard error.
held_row <- fit_tight$theta_levels$theta_name %in% held
stopifnot(length(held) == 1, fit_tight$theta[[held]] == 5, fit_profiled$theta[[held]] > 5,
          fit_tight$ofv > fit_profiled$ofv, isTRUE(fit_tight$converged),
          is.na(fit_tight$theta_levels$se[held_row]), is.na(fit_tight$estimates[held, "se"]), all(is.finite(fit_tight$theta_levels$se[!held_row])),
          "boundary_estimate" %in% ferx_get_warnings(fit_tight, as_df = TRUE)$category)
# The prose: fit$held_at_bound names the held level as a profiled bound, ferx-r does not report it
# as a non-positive variance, and its correlations are NA.
held_variance_warning <- character(0)
withCallingHandlers(ferx_fit(tight_model, mbma$data, verbose = FALSE),
                    warning = function(w) {
                      held_variance_warning <<- c(held_variance_warning, conditionMessage(w))
                      invokeRestart("muffleWarning")
                    })
stopifnot(!any(grepl("Non-positive variance", held_variance_warning, fixed = TRUE)),
          identical(fit_tight$profiled_levels_at_bound, held),
          identical(fit_tight$held_at_bound$reason, "profiled_bound"),
          all(is.na(fit_tight$cor_matrix[held, colnames(fit_tight$cor_matrix) != held])))
# The sentence on a box no level reaches: the same fit to the optimizer's tolerance, not bit for bit.
unbounded_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_fixed_study_profiled_unbounded.ferx")
writeLines(sub("contrast = sum_to_zero](0.0, -50.0, 50.0) profile", "contrast = sum_to_zero](0.0) profile",
               profiled_lines, fixed = TRUE), unbounded_model)
fit_unbounded <- ferx_fit(unbounded_model, mbma$data, verbose = FALSE)
box_gap <- max(abs(fit_unbounded$theta - fit_profiled$theta))
stopifnot(!identical(fit_unbounded$theta, fit_profiled$theta), box_gap < 1e-4,
          abs(fit_unbounded$ofv - fit_profiled$ofv) < 1e-8)
```

Unbounded, `r held` is `r sprintf("%.2f", fit_profiled$theta[[held]])`. With the box, the solve stops it on the bound and re-solves the other levels with it held there, so the objective rises by `r sprintf("%.2f", fit_tight$ofv - fit_profiled$ofv)`. `fit$held_at_bound`, printed first above, lists it with the reason `profiled_bound`; it lists every parameter the covariance step gives no standard error, a profiled level on its bound among them. A `boundary_estimate` warning reports it as well. `fit$profiled_levels_at_bound` still names the held level, but it is deprecated in favour of `held_at_bound`. The covariance step holds it as it holds a `FIX` theta: its standard error is `NA` in `theta_levels` and `fit$estimates` (and `N/A` in the THETA table of a block small enough to print in full), and every other standard error is computed with it held. The bounds apply to the free coefficients, so under a sum-to-zero contrast the derived level, which has no theta, is never held.

A level on its bound says that the bound, not the data, decides its value: relax the bound unless it encodes something you know. A box that no level reaches changes nothing that matters. Dropping the `−50` to `50` bounds altogether moves the estimates by at most `r signif(box_gap, 1)`, well within the optimizer's tolerance (ferx-core's [bounds on a profiled block](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/parameters.html#bounds-on-a-profiled-block) describe the two fits as identical to the bit, which at this build they are not quite).

`profile` needs FOCE, FOCEI or Laplace (with or without adaptive quadrature, `n_agq`) and, on a continuous endpoint, an additive residual error, and it rules out priors and `global_search`, among others. ferx refuses each such fit with `E_PROFILE_SCOPE`. A residual `correlation` line, shown in the next section, is allowed. See [profiled level blocks](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/parameters.html#profiled-level-blocks) in ferx-core for the full list.

#### A responder endpoint {#sec-mbma-responder}

Many trials report a responder rate per arm and visit instead of a mean: `r` of `n` patients responded. A `[binary_model]` predictor (@sec-binary) can read a theta level block, so the same unstructured placebo time course carries over to the log-odds, and that block can be profiled too. The responder counts here are simulated from the bundled design, with its studies, arms, visits and arm sizes. The log-odds is a study effect plus a placebo time course that rises over the visits, with an active arm adding a constant after week 0:

```{r}
#| label: responder-data
set.seed(2604)
resp_cells <- distinct(arm_data, STUDY, TIME) |>
  mutate(placebo = 0.8 * (1 - exp(-TIME / 3)) + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.2))
study_logit <- rnorm(n_distinct(arm_data$STUDY), -1.2, 0.4)
resp_arms <- arm_data |>
  select(STUDY, OCC, TIME, DOSE, NARM) |>
  left_join(resp_cells, by = c("STUDY", "TIME")) |>
  mutate(TRT = as.numeric(DOSE > 0 & TIME > 0),
         RESP = rbinom(n(), NARM, plogis(study_logit[STUDY] + placebo + 0.8 * TRT)))
head(select(resp_arms, STUDY, OCC, TIME, DOSE, NARM, RESP), 5)
```

ferx scores a binary endpoint one record at a time, so each arm and visit becomes `NARM` rows, `RESP` of them with `DV = 1`. All rows of a cell share its probability, so their likelihood is the binomial likelihood of the count, up to a constant. `ID` is the study, as in the continuous data:

```{r}
#| label: responder-rows
resp_data <- resp_arms |>
  slice(rep(seq_len(n()), NARM)) |>
  group_by(STUDY, OCC, TIME) |>
  mutate(DV = as.numeric(row_number() <= RESP)) |>
  ungroup() |>
  transmute(ID = STUDY, STUDY, TIME, DV, CMT = 1, EVID = 0, MDV = 0, TRT) |>
  arrange(ID, TIME)
stopifnot(nrow(resp_data) == sum(resp_arms$NARM), sum(resp_data$DV) == sum(resp_arms$RESP))
nrow(resp_data)
```

The model reads `PLACEBO` in the `logit` line of `[binary_model]`, whose link to the probability is implicit, with a study random effect and a treatment shift on the log-odds:

```{r}
#| label: responder-model
resp_lines <- c(
  "[parameters]",
  "  theta TVL(-1.0, -5.0, 5.0)",
  "  theta EMAX(0.5, -5.0, 5.0)",
  "  theta PLACEBO[STUDY, TIME, contrast = sum_to_zero_within](0.0, -10.0, 10.0)",
  "  omega ETA_S ~ 0.25",
  "",
  "[covariates]",
  "  STUDY categorical",
  "  TRT   continuous",
  "",
  "[binary_model]",
  "  cmt   = 1",
  "  logit = TVL + PLACEBO + ETA_S + EMAX * TRT",
  "",
  "[fit_options]",
  "  method = focei")
resp_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_responder.ferx")
writeLines(resp_lines, resp_model)
fit_resp <- ferx_fit(resp_model, resp_data, verbose = FALSE)
c(converged = fit_resp$converged, covariance = fit_resp$covariance_status)
fit_resp$theta[c("TVL", "EMAX")]
head(fit_resp$theta_levels, 4)
```

Declared `profile`, the block is solved at every step as before:

```{r}
#| label: responder-profile
resp_profiled_lines <- sub("(0.0, -10.0, 10.0)", "(0.0, -10.0, 10.0) profile", resp_lines, fixed = TRUE)
stopifnot(any(grepl("sum_to_zero_within](0.0, -10.0, 10.0) profile", resp_profiled_lines, fixed = TRUE)))
resp_profiled_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_responder_profiled.ferx")
writeLines(resp_profiled_lines, resp_profiled_model)
fit_resp_profiled <- ferx_fit(resp_profiled_model, resp_data, verbose = FALSE)
fit_resp_profiled$profiled_blocks
data.frame(levels = c("estimated", "profiled"),
           ofv = c(fit_resp$ofv, fit_resp_profiled$ofv),
           n_parameters = c(fit_resp$n_parameters, fit_resp_profiled$n_parameters),
           seconds = round(c(fit_resp$wall_time_secs, fit_resp_profiled$wall_time_secs), 2))
rbind(estimated = fit_resp$theta[c("TVL", "EMAX")], profiled = fit_resp_profiled$theta[c("TVL", "EMAX")])
```

```{r}
#| label: check-responder-profile
#| include: false
# profiled_pair_gap() backs the prose shared by the logit pair here and the probit pair below: both
# fits converge with a computed covariance step; the same objective to the printed digits (measured at
# the pin on macOS: 7e-10 for logit, 4.5e-10 for probit, stated inline; the check allows up to 1e-6,
# and the prose relies on a nonzero gap for its "e" format) and the same parameter count; every
# estimate, levels and the ETA_S variance included, within 1% of its standard error; every level
# flagged profiled and none on a bound. It returns the OFV gap.
# Every slot is checked for presence first: NULL == "computed", all(NULL) and !any(NULL) all pass.
profiled_pair_gap <- function(est, prof) {
  est_flags <- est$theta_levels$profiled
  prof_flags <- prof$theta_levels$profiled
  stopifnot(isTRUE(est$converged), isTRUE(prof$converged),
            identical(est$covariance_status, "computed"), identical(prof$covariance_status, "computed"),
            identical(prof$profiled_blocks, "PLACEBO"),
            is.logical(prof_flags), length(prof_flags) > 0, length(prof_flags) == nrow(prof$theta_levels),
            all(prof_flags),
            is.logical(est_flags), length(est_flags) == nrow(est$theta_levels), !any(est_flags),
            is.character(prof$profiled_levels_at_bound), length(prof$profiled_levels_at_bound) == 0,
            length(est$n_parameters) == 1, length(prof$n_parameters) == 1,
            prof$n_parameters == est$n_parameters,
            length(est$ofv) == 1, length(prof$ofv) == 1)
  gap <- abs(prof$ofv - est$ofv)
  stopifnot(signif(prof$ofv, 7) == signif(est$ofv, 7), gap > 0, gap < 1e-6,
            length(est$theta) > 0, length(est$se_theta) == length(est$theta),
            identical(names(prof$theta), names(est$theta)),
            all(abs(prof$theta - est$theta) < 0.01 * est$se_theta),
            # "levels included": fit$theta holds only the free levels; theta_levels has the derived ones too.
            identical(prof$theta_levels$label, est$theta_levels$label),
            length(est$theta_levels$se) == nrow(est$theta_levels),
            all(abs(prof$theta_levels$value - est$theta_levels$value) < 0.01 * est$theta_levels$se),
            # "every estimate" includes the ETA_S variance.
            length(est$se_omega) == 1,
            all(abs(diag(as.matrix(prof$omega)) - diag(as.matrix(est$omega))) < 0.01 * est$se_omega))
  gap
}
resp_gap <- profiled_pair_gap(fit_resp, fit_resp_profiled)
# The prose: the profiled fit is slower on this small block (only the direction is checked: the
# ratio itself moves with machine load).
stopifnot(length(fit_resp$wall_time_secs) == 1, length(fit_resp_profiled$wall_time_secs) == 1,
          fit_resp_profiled$wall_time_secs > fit_resp$wall_time_secs)
```

Both fits converge, and the profiled one reaches the same objective to the printed digits: the two are `r sprintf("%.0e", resp_gap)` OFV units apart, and every estimate, levels included, moves by less than 1% of its standard error. `fit$profiled_blocks` names the block, the `profiled` column of `theta_levels` marks all `r nrow(fit_resp_profiled$theta_levels)` levels, and `n_parameters` is the same, so the profiled fit's BIC and likelihood-ratio tests are those of the estimated one. As in the continuous model, profiling does not pay off on a block this small: on `r format(nrow(resp_data), big.mark = ",")` rows it took `r sprintf("%.1f", fit_resp_profiled$wall_time_secs / fit_resp$wall_time_secs)` times as long when this page was rendered.

`[binary_model]` takes a logit or a probit link. Written as `probit =` instead of `logit =`, the predictor gives the probability through the standard-normal CDF, P(DV = 1) = Φ(predictor); `link = probit` may be added, but the key implies it (see [the probit link](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/categorical.html#the-probit-link) in ferx-core). A profiled block is read the same way under either link. The same responder data under a probit link, with the block estimated and profiled:

```{r}
#| label: responder-probit
probit_lines <- sub("  logit = ", "  probit = ", resp_lines, fixed = TRUE)
probit_profiled_lines <- sub("  logit = ", "  probit = ", resp_profiled_lines, fixed = TRUE)
stopifnot(sum(startsWith(probit_lines, "  probit = ")) == 1,
          sum(startsWith(probit_profiled_lines, "  probit = ")) == 1)
probit_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_responder_probit.ferx")
probit_profiled_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_responder_probit_profiled.ferx")
writeLines(probit_lines, probit_model)
writeLines(probit_profiled_lines, probit_profiled_model)
fit_probit <- ferx_fit(probit_model, resp_data, verbose = FALSE)
fit_probit_profiled <- ferx_fit(probit_profiled_model, resp_data, verbose = FALSE)
fit_probit_profiled$profiled_blocks
data.frame(link = c("logit", "probit", "probit"), levels = c("estimated", "estimated", "profiled"),
           converged = c(fit_resp$converged, fit_probit$converged, fit_probit_profiled$converged),
           ofv = c(fit_resp$ofv, fit_probit$ofv, fit_probit_profiled$ofv),
           n_parameters = c(fit_resp$n_parameters, fit_probit$n_parameters, fit_probit_profiled$n_parameters))
rbind(logit = fit_resp$theta[c("TVL", "EMAX")], probit = fit_probit$theta[c("TVL", "EMAX")],
      probit_profiled = fit_probit_profiled$theta[c("TVL", "EMAX")])
typical_arm <- rbind(
  logit = plogis(fit_resp$theta[["TVL"]] + c(placebo = 0, active = fit_resp$theta[["EMAX"]])),
  probit = pnorm(fit_probit$theta[["TVL"]] + c(placebo = 0, active = fit_probit$theta[["EMAX"]])))
round(typical_arm, 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-responder-probit
#| include: false
# The prose: the probit pair passes profiled_pair_gap() (defined in check-responder-profile), with
# the same parameter count as the logit fit; the logit coefficients are 1.5 to 1.75 times the probit
# ones; the typical-arm probabilities agree; the OFVs of the two links are close.
probit_gap <- profiled_pair_gap(fit_probit, fit_probit_profiled)
stopifnot(length(fit_resp$n_parameters) == 1, fit_probit$n_parameters == fit_resp$n_parameters)
# "close to the factor of about 1.6 to 1.8": measured 1.62 (TVL) and 1.61 (EMAX); a band that a
# ratio of 1.85 (pi / sqrt(3)) or 1.0 (a probit key read as logit) fails.
probit_ratio <- fit_resp$theta[c("TVL", "EMAX")] / fit_probit$theta[c("TVL", "EMAX")]
stopifnot(all(probit_ratio > 1.5), all(probit_ratio < 1.75))
# "the probabilities agree to within 0.01" at the typical arm (measured: 0.0014 and 0.0006).
stopifnot(all(dim(typical_arm) == c(2, 2)), max(abs(typical_arm["logit", ] - typical_arm["probit", ])) < 0.01)
# "the two links cannot be told apart here": the OFVs differ by much less than one unit (measured 0.19)
# at the same parameter count.
probit_ofv_gap <- fit_resp$ofv - fit_probit$ofv
stopifnot(abs(probit_ofv_gap) < 1)
```

Both probit fits converge, and the profiled one is `r sprintf("%.0e", probit_gap)` OFV units from the estimated one, with every estimate, levels included, within 1% of its standard error and all `r nrow(fit_probit_profiled$theta_levels)` levels flagged `profiled`. The two links put the coefficients on different scales: here the logit `TVL` is `r round(probit_ratio[["TVL"]], 2)` times the probit one and the logit `EMAX` `r round(probit_ratio[["EMAX"]], 2)` times, close to the factor of about 1.6 to 1.8 often used to convert between the two. Compare probabilities, not coefficients, across links: at a typical arm (no study effect, placebo at its study mean) the two fits give probabilities within 0.01 of each other, on placebo and on the active arm. The probit OFV is `r round(abs(probit_ofv_gap), 2)` units `r if (probit_ofv_gap > 0) "lower" else "higher"` with the same number of parameters, so on these data, simulated under a logit link, the two links cannot be told apart.

The predictor must read the block as a coefficient times the block plus terms that do not read it, the same rule as inside `inv_logit()` (see [through a link](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/parameters.html#through-a-link) in ferx-core).

#### An observed proportion through `pnorm()` {#sec-mbma-proportion}

A publication may report only the proportion of responders per arm and visit, with its standard error, and not the counts. That is a bounded continuous endpoint: one row per arm and visit, as in the score data, with a prediction that must stay between 0 and 1. The probit link is then written into the model: `pnorm()` is the standard-normal CDF Φ, the same function as R's `pnorm()`, and `y = pnorm(LP)` keeps the prediction in (0, 1) whatever the linear predictor `LP`. It is the probit counterpart of `y = inv_logit(LP)`, and a level block inside it can be profiled.

The proportions here are simulated on the bundled design under a probit link: a study effect and a placebo time course on the probit scale, with an active arm adding a constant, `prop_emax`, after week 0. Each arm's observed proportion is a binomial count divided by `NARM`, and its standard error is the one a publication would print, √(p(1 − p) / `NARM`) at the observed p:

```{r}
#| label: proportion-data
set.seed(2605)
prop_cells <- distinct(arm_data, STUDY, TIME) |>
  mutate(placebo = 0.5 * (1 - exp(-TIME / 3)) + rnorm(n(), 0, 0.12))
study_probit <- rnorm(n_distinct(arm_data$STUDY), -0.7, 0.25)
prop_emax <- 0.5
prop_data <- arm_data |>
  select(ID, STUDY, OCC, TIME, DOSE, NARM) |>
  left_join(prop_cells, by = c("STUDY", "TIME")) |>
  mutate(TRT = as.numeric(DOSE > 0 & TIME > 0),
         DV = rbinom(n(), NARM, pnorm(study_probit[STUDY] + placebo + prop_emax * TRT)) / NARM,
         SE = sqrt(DV * (1 - DV) / NARM), MDV = 0) |>
  select(ID, STUDY, OCC, TIME, DV, MDV, SE, NARM, TRT)
stopifnot(all(prop_data$DV > 0 & prop_data$DV < 1))
head(prop_data, 4)
range(prop_data$DV)
```

An observed proportion of exactly 0 or 1 would get a standard error of 0, and so an infinite weight; the `stopifnot()` confirms none occurs here. The model is the score model's layout, with the linear predictor in `[individual_parameters]` and the link around the whole prediction. Weighting is as before, `weight = SE` with `ADD_ERR` fixed at 1:

```{r}
#| label: proportion-model
prop_lines <- c(
  "[parameters]",
  "  theta TVL(-0.5, -5.0, 5.0)",
  "  theta EMAX(0.3, -5.0, 5.0)",
  "  theta PLACEBO[STUDY, TIME, contrast = sum_to_zero_within](0.0, -5.0, 5.0)",
  "  omega ETA_S ~ 0.1",
  "  sigma ADD_ERR ~ 1.0 (variance) FIX",
  "",
  "[covariates]",
  "  STUDY categorical",
  "  SE    continuous",
  "  TRT   continuous",
  "",
  "[individual_parameters]",
  "  LP = TVL + PLACEBO + ETA_S + EMAX * TRT",
  "",
  "[structural_model]",
  "  y = pnorm(LP)",
  "",
  "[error_model]",
  "  DV ~ additive(ADD_ERR) weight = SE",
  "",
  "[fit_options]",
  "  method = focei")
prop_profiled_lines <- sub("(0.0, -5.0, 5.0)", "(0.0, -5.0, 5.0) profile", prop_lines, fixed = TRUE)
stopifnot(any(grepl("sum_to_zero_within](0.0, -5.0, 5.0) profile", prop_profiled_lines, fixed = TRUE)))
prop_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_proportion_probit.ferx")
prop_profiled_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_proportion_probit_profiled.ferx")
writeLines(prop_lines, prop_model)
writeLines(prop_profiled_lines, prop_profiled_model)
fit_prop <- ferx_fit(prop_model, prop_data, verbose = FALSE)
fit_prop_profiled <- ferx_fit(prop_profiled_model, prop_data, verbose = FALSE)
fit_prop_profiled$profiled_blocks
data.frame(levels = c("estimated", "profiled"),
           converged = c(fit_prop$converged, fit_prop_profiled$converged),
           ofv = c(fit_prop$ofv, fit_prop_profiled$ofv),
           n_parameters = c(fit_prop$n_parameters, fit_prop_profiled$n_parameters))
data.frame(estimated = fit_prop$theta[c("TVL", "EMAX")], se = fit_prop$se_theta[c("TVL", "EMAX")],
           profiled = fit_prop_profiled$theta[c("TVL", "EMAX")])
```

The population prediction is Φ of the typical linear predictor, `TVL` plus the row's placebo level plus `EMAX` for an active arm after week 0, so it can be rebuilt from the estimates with R's `pnorm()`:

```{r}
#| label: proportion-pred
prop_levels <- setNames(fit_prop$theta_levels$value, fit_prop$theta_levels$label)
prop_lp <- fit_prop$theta[["TVL"]] + prop_levels[paste0("STUDY=", prop_data$STUDY, ",TIME=", prop_data$TIME)] +
  fit_prop$theta[["EMAX"]] * prop_data$TRT
all.equal(fit_prop$sdtab$PRED, unname(pnorm(prop_lp)))
range(fit_prop$sdtab$IPRED)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-proportion-probit
#| include: false
# The prose: the pair passes profiled_pair_gap() (defined in check-responder-profile; measured at the
# pin on macOS: gap 1.2e-10, every estimate within 3e-6 of its SE), PRED is pnorm() of the typical
# linear predictor (all.equal above must hold, not just print), IPRED stays inside (0, 1), and EMAX
# recovers the simulated 0.5 within its 95% interval. A pnorm() read as inv_logit() puts EMAX near
# 0.8 (1.6 times), outside that interval, and fails the PRED identity.
prop_gap <- profiled_pair_gap(fit_prop, fit_prop_profiled)
stopifnot(nrow(fit_prop$sdtab) == nrow(prop_data), length(prop_lp) == nrow(prop_data),
          isTRUE(all.equal(fit_prop$sdtab$PRED, unname(pnorm(prop_lp)))),
          length(fit_prop$sdtab$IPRED) == nrow(prop_data),
          all(fit_prop$sdtab$IPRED > 0 & fit_prop$sdtab$IPRED < 1),
          abs(fit_prop$theta[["EMAX"]] - prop_emax) < 1.96 * fit_prop$se_theta[["EMAX"]],
          abs(fit_prop_profiled$theta[["EMAX"]] - prop_emax) < 1.96 * fit_prop$se_theta[["EMAX"]])
```

Both fits converge with a computed covariance step. The profiled one is `r sprintf("%.0e", prop_gap)` OFV units from the estimated one, every estimate, levels and the `ETA_S` variance included, is within 1% of its standard error, and all `r nrow(fit_prop_profiled$theta_levels)` levels are flagged `profiled`. `EMAX`, `r sprintf("%.3f", fit_prop$theta[["EMAX"]])` (standard error `r sprintf("%.3f", fit_prop$se_theta[["EMAX"]])`), recovers the simulated `r prop_emax` on the probit scale, and the population prediction equals R's `pnorm()` of the typical linear predictor. Writing `inv_logit(LP)` instead of `pnorm(LP)` gives the logit form, whose coefficients are on the logit scale; compare the two links through their probabilities, as for the responder fits above.

## Correlated residuals within an arm

The model scores an arm's visits as independent once its random effects are known: the kappa shifts every visit of an arm by the same amount, and what is left is independent. Arm means of one study arm over time can be correlated beyond that, for instance because the same patients are measured at every visit. A `correlation` line in `[error_model]` lets the residuals of the rows of one group correlate. Its parameter is an ordinary theta that only the line reads.

Compound symmetry, `cs`, correlates every two rows of a group equally, and on this model that is the same covariance as the arm kappa. ferx therefore refuses `cs` grouped by the arm while a kappa is drawn per arm:

```{r}
#| label: correlation-cs
add_correlation <- function(lines, structure, lower = "0.0") {
  lines <- sub("  sigma ADD_ERR", sprintf("  theta RHO(0.3, %s, 0.95)\n  sigma ADD_ERR", lower), lines, fixed = TRUE)
  sub("DV ~ additive(ADD_ERR) weight = SE",
      sprintf("DV ~ additive(ADD_ERR) weight = SE\n  correlation %s(RHO) by OCC", structure), lines, fixed = TRUE)
}
cs_lines <- add_correlation(readLines(mbma$model), "cs", lower = "-0.2")
stopifnot(any(grepl("theta RHO(0.3, -0.2, 0.95)", cs_lines, fixed = TRUE)),
          any(grepl("correlation cs(RHO) by OCC", cs_lines, fixed = TRUE)))
cs_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_cs.ferx")
writeLines(cs_lines, cs_model)
try(ferx_fit(cs_model, mbma$data, verbose = FALSE))
```

`car1`, the continuous-time first-order autoregressive structure, correlates two visits at times $t_a$ and $t_b$ by $\rho^{|t_a - t_b|}$, so the correlation decays with the weeks between them, while the kappa keeps the part all visits share. Its `ρ` must lie in $[0, 1)$, hence the bounds 0 to 0.95:

```{r}
#| label: correlation-car1
car1_lines <- add_correlation(readLines(mbma$model), "car1")
stopifnot(any(grepl("theta RHO(0.3, 0.0, 0.95)", car1_lines, fixed = TRUE)),
          any(grepl("correlation car1(RHO) by OCC", car1_lines, fixed = TRUE)))
car1_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_car1.ferx")
writeLines(car1_lines, car1_model)
fit_car1 <- ferx_fit(car1_model, mbma$data, verbose = FALSE)
grep("Residual:|^RHO", capture.output(print(fit_car1)), value = TRUE)
data.frame(residuals = c("independent", "car1 by OCC"),
           ofv = c(fit$ofv, fit_car1$ofv), n_parameters = c(fit$n_parameters, fit_car1$n_parameters),
           rho = c(NA, fit_car1$theta[["RHO"]]),
           gamma2 = c(fit$omega_iov[1, 1], fit_car1$omega_iov[1, 1]))
```

```{r}
#| label: check-correlation-car1
#| include: false
# The prose: cs is refused as confounded with the arm kappa; car1 converges one parameter up,
# lowers the OFV by more than the chi-square 5% value, and lowers gamma^2.
cs_code <- tryCatch({ ferx_fit(cs_model, mbma$data, verbose = FALSE); NULL }, error = function(e) e$code)
stopifnot(identical(cs_code, "E_RESIDUAL_CORRELATION_CONFOUNDED_KAPPA"), isTRUE(fit_car1$converged),
          fit_car1$n_parameters == fit$n_parameters + 1, fit$ofv - fit_car1$ofv > qchisq(0.95, 1),
          fit_car1$omega_iov[1, 1] < fit$omega_iov[1, 1])
```

The correlation costs one parameter and lowers the OFV by `r sprintf("%.1f", fit$ofv - fit_car1$ofv)`. At `ρ` = `r sprintf("%.2f", fit_car1$theta[["RHO"]])`, two visits two weeks apart correlate by `r sprintf("%.2f", fit_car1$theta[["RHO"]]^2)`, and γ² falls a little, since the line now carries part of what visits of one arm share. Read against a χ² distribution with one degree of freedom, the drop would be significant. But the generator draws every visit of an arm independently, so there is no serial correlation to find. The reference distribution is what is wrong. Simulating from the fit without the line, and fitting each simulated study with and without it, shows the drops such a test produces when there is no correlation:

```{r}
#| label: correlation-null
null_sims <- ferx_simulate(mbma$model, mbma$data, n_sim = 50, seed = 1, fit = fit)
# suppress the R warning that reports overriding the model file's covariance setting
null_drops <- suppressWarnings(sapply(1:50, function(i) {
  sim_rows <- null_sims[null_sims$SIM == i, ]
  stopifnot(all(sim_rows$ID == arm_data$ID), all(sim_rows$TIME == arm_data$TIME))
  sim_data <- mutate(arm_data, DV = sim_rows$DV_SIM)
  ferx_fit(mbma$model, sim_data, covariance = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)$ofv -
    ferx_fit(car1_model, sim_data, covariance = FALSE, verbose = FALSE)$ofv
}))
c(at_least_observed = mean(null_drops >= fit$ofv - fit_car1$ofv),
  above_chisq_5pct = mean(null_drops >= qchisq(0.95, 1)))
```

```{r}
#| label: check-correlation-null
#| include: false
# The prose: the observed drop is not in the top 5% of the null drops, and far more than 5% of
# the null drops exceed the chi-square critical value.
stopifnot(mean(null_drops >= fit$ofv - fit_car1$ofv) >= 0.05, mean(null_drops >= qchisq(0.95, 1)) > 0.15)
```

`r sum(null_drops >= fit$ofv - fit_car1$ofv)` of the 50 simulated meta-analyses without any correlation give a drop at least as large as the observed one, and `r round(100 * mean(null_drops >= qchisq(0.95, 1)))`% exceed `r sprintf("%.2f", qchisq(0.95, 1))`, the χ² critical value that only 5% should exceed. With six studies and 22 arms, the likelihood-ratio test of `ρ` is far too liberal, and the observed drop is no evidence of serial correlation. Calibrate such a test by simulation, as here, before adding a correlation line to a meta-analysis of few studies. When the visits are one time unit apart, `car1` is the same as `ar1`, which counts visits rather than weeks; ferx-core's [residual correlation](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/residual-correlation.html) page describes both.

A correlation line combines with a profiled block. Profiling the bundled block beside `car1` gives the same fit:

```{r}
#| label: correlation-profiled
car1_profiled_lines <- sub("contrast = sum_to_zero_within](0.0, -50.0, 50.0)",
                           "contrast = sum_to_zero_within](0.0, -50.0, 50.0) profile", car1_lines, fixed = TRUE)
stopifnot(any(grepl("sum_to_zero_within](0.0, -50.0, 50.0) profile", car1_profiled_lines, fixed = TRUE)))
car1_profiled_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_car1_profiled.ferx")
writeLines(car1_profiled_lines, car1_profiled_model)
fit_car1_profiled <- ferx_fit(car1_profiled_model, mbma$data, verbose = FALSE)
c(estimated = fit_car1$ofv, profiled = fit_car1_profiled$ofv)
rbind(estimated = fit_car1$theta[c(1:4, which(names(fit_car1$theta) == "RHO"))],
      profiled = fit_car1_profiled$theta[c(1:4, which(names(fit_car1_profiled$theta) == "RHO"))])
```

```{r}
#| label: check-correlation-profiled
#| include: false
stopifnot(isTRUE(fit_car1_profiled$converged), abs(fit_car1_profiled$ofv - fit_car1$ofv) < 1e-3,
          abs(fit_car1_profiled$theta[["RHO"]] - fit_car1$theta[["RHO"]]) < 1e-3)
```

## Checking the treatment contrast

An MBMA is about the treatment contrast: the difference between an active arm and placebo within a study. An arm-level VPC (@sec-vpc) mixes that with everything else the arms of a study share, above all the between-study spread. `ferx_contrast_vpc()` forms the contrast directly. Within each study (`within`) and visit (`time`, `TIME` by default), it subtracts the reference arm (`by` equal to `ref`) from each active arm, on the data and on every replicate of a simulation from the fit. The between-study `ETA_E0` and the placebo levels are shared by a study's arms and cancel, so what is left is the drug effect plus the between-arm and residual variability. `arm` names the column that tells a study's arms apart (`OCC` here):

```{r}
#| label: contrast-vpc
contrast <- ferx_contrast_vpc(fit, by = "DOSE", ref = 0, within = "ID", arm = "OCC",
                              n_sim = 500, seed = 1)
contrast
head(contrast$pairs, 4)
```

`print()` on a `ferx_contrast_vpc` object summarises the pairing and the check. `$pairs` has one row per study, visit and active arm: the observed contrast, the simulated band for that pair (`SIM_LO`, `SIM_MED`, `SIM_HI`, at `probs`, by default the 5th, 50th and 95th percentiles) and `PCTL`, the fraction of simulated contrasts below the observed one. `$vpc` summarises by dose and visit, and `plot()` draws it:

```{r}
#| label: fig-contrast-vpc
#| fig-cap: "Contrast VPC: active minus placebo within a study, by dose and week. Points are observed contrasts, the band is the 90% interval of the simulated median contrast."
#| fig-height: 6
plot(contrast)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-contrast-vpc
#| include: false
# The prose counts pairs, studies and the cells whose observed median falls outside the band.
outside <- with(contrast$vpc, OBS_MED < SIM_LO | OBS_MED > SIM_HI)
extreme <- with(contrast$pairs, PCTL < 0.05 | PCTL > 0.95)
stopifnot(nrow(contrast$pairs) > 0, length(contrast$excluded) == 0,
          sum(outside) < nrow(contrast$vpc) / 4)
```

The `r nrow(contrast$pairs)` pairs come from all `r length(unique(contrast$pairs$ID))` studies, since each has a placebo arm at every visit. The observed median contrast lies outside the simulated band in `r sum(outside)` of the `r nrow(contrast$vpc)` dose-by-week cells, and `r sum(extreme)` of the `r nrow(contrast$pairs)` single pairs fall outside their own 5 to 95 percent range. With one to five pairs per cell and a 90% band, a few such cells are expected by chance; a dose-response or time course the model gets wrong would show as a run of cells on one side.

Other arguments: `scale` sets the scale the difference is formed on (`"observed"`, the default, or `"log"`, `"logit"`, `"expit"`), `cmt` picks one endpoint of multi-endpoint data, and `model` and `data` override the fit's own files. A study without a reference arm is left out with a warning, and one with two reference arms is refused.

## Nested levels: sponsor, study and arm

So far each study is a subject: `ETA_E0` is between-study variability, and the kappa, drawn once per arm, is between-arm variability. A meta-analysis can have one more grouping, such as several studies run by one sponsor, whose studies resemble each other more than studies of different sponsors. ferx declares such groupings as nested levels below the subject. The subject (`ID`) is the coarsest group, and `level NAME by COLUMN in PARENT` declares each finer one. Each kappa says at which level it is drawn, so a kappa `at STUDY` is shared by the arms of a study and a kappa `at ARM` is drawn once per arm.

The bundled studies have no sponsor. To show the layout, pair them into three sponsors (studies 1-2, 3-4 and 5-6). The pairing is arbitrary: the generator draws every study independently. `ID` becomes the sponsor, and `ARM` copies `OCC`. Level labels are nested by key, so arm 1 of study 1 and arm 1 of study 2 are different arms. A subject's rows must be adjacent: the data are sorted by `ID`, as they would have to be after any other pairing:

```{r}
#| label: nested-data
nested_data <- arm_data |>
  mutate(SPONSOR = c(1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 3)[STUDY], ID = SPONSOR, ARM = OCC) |>
  arrange(ID, STUDY)
nested_data |> distinct(ID, STUDY) |> count(ID, name = "studies")
```

The placebo block stays as it is. Each level of `PLACEBO[STUDY, TIME]` lies inside one study, so the block could absorb a study kappa. ferx checks this when it binds the levels, and under `sum_to_zero_within` the block's levels sum to zero within each study, which leaves each study's mean to the kappa, as it left it to `ETA_E0` before. Two models follow: the bundled model written with levels (the study kappa `K_ST` in place of `ETA_E0`, no sponsor effect), and that model with a sponsor random effect `ETA_SP`:

```{r}
#| label: nested-models
level_lines <- readLines(mbma$model)
level_lines <- level_lines[!grepl("^\\s*iov_column", level_lines)]
level_lines <- sub("omega ETA_E0 ~ 4.0 (sd)",
                   "level STUDY by STUDY in ID\n  level ARM by ARM in STUDY\n  kappa K_ST ~ 4.0 (sd) at STUDY",
                   level_lines, fixed = TRUE)
level_lines <- sub("weight = NARM", "at ARM weight = NARM", level_lines, fixed = TRUE)
level_lines <- sub("BASE = TVE0 + PLACEBO + ETA_E0 + KAPPA_ARM", "BASE = TVE0 + PLACEBO + K_ST + KAPPA_ARM",
                   level_lines, fixed = TRUE)
sponsor_lines <- sub("level STUDY by STUDY in ID", "omega ETA_SP ~ 4.0 (sd)\n  level STUDY by STUDY in ID",
                     level_lines, fixed = TRUE)
sponsor_lines <- sub("BASE = TVE0 + PLACEBO + K_ST", "BASE = TVE0 + PLACEBO + ETA_SP + K_ST", sponsor_lines, fixed = TRUE)
# Stop unless every edit landed.
stopifnot(!any(grepl("^[^#]*ETA_E0", level_lines)), !any(grepl("^\\s*iov_column", level_lines)),
          any(grepl("^\\s*kappa KAPPA_ARM.*at ARM weight = NARM", level_lines)),
          any(grepl("ETA_SP + K_ST + KAPPA_ARM", sponsor_lines, fixed = TRUE)))
study_level_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_levels.ferx")
writeLines(level_lines, study_level_model)
sponsor_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_levels_sponsor.ferx")
writeLines(sponsor_lines, sponsor_model)
invisible(ferx_model_get_section(sponsor_model, "parameters"))

fit_levels <- ferx_fit(study_level_model, nested_data, verbose = FALSE)
fit_sponsor <- ferx_fit(sponsor_model, nested_data, verbose = FALSE)
data.frame(model = c("bundled (one level)", "levels, no sponsor effect", "levels with sponsor effect"),
           converged = c(fit$converged, fit_levels$converged, fit_sponsor$converged),
           ofv = c(fit$ofv, fit_levels$ofv, fit_sponsor$ofv),
           n_parameters = c(fit$n_parameters, fit_levels$n_parameters, fit_sponsor$n_parameters),
           sponsor_var = c(NA, NA, fit_sponsor$omega[1, 1]),
           study_var = c(fit$omega[1, 1], fit_levels$omega_iov[1, 1], fit_sponsor$omega_iov[1, 1]),
           arm_gamma2 = c(fit$omega_iov[1, 1], fit_levels$omega_iov[2, 2], fit_sponsor$omega_iov[2, 2]))
```

```{r}
#| label: check-nested-models
#| include: false
# The prose: the levelled model without a sponsor effect is the bundled model (same objective,
# study kappa = ETA_E0, same arm gamma^2, same placebo levels); the sponsor fit is lower by a few
# OFV points with one more parameter, and the sponsor variance takes the between-study variance,
# leaving a study kappa collapsed at the optimizer's guard and highly shrunk.
sponsor_warnings <- ferx_get_warnings(fit_sponsor, as_df = TRUE)
stopifnot(fit$converged, fit_levels$converged, fit_sponsor$converged,
          abs(fit_levels$ofv - fit$ofv) < 1e-3,
          abs(fit_levels$omega_iov[1, 1] / fit$omega[1, 1] - 1) < 1e-3,
          abs(fit_levels$omega_iov[2, 2] / fit$omega_iov[1, 1] - 1) < 1e-3,
          isTRUE(all.equal(fit_levels$theta_levels$value, fit$theta_levels$value, tolerance = 1e-3)),
          fit_levels$n_parameters == fit$n_parameters, fit_sponsor$n_parameters == fit$n_parameters + 1,
          fit_sponsor$ofv < fit$ofv, fit$ofv - fit_sponsor$ofv < 10,
          fit_sponsor$omega[1, 1] > 5 * fit_sponsor$omega_iov[1, 1],
          fit_sponsor$shrinkage_kappa[["K_ST"]] > 0.3,
          any(sponsor_warnings$category == "parameter_at_runaway_guard" & grepl("K_ST", sponsor_warnings$message)),
          identical(fit_sponsor$kappa_levels, c(K_ST = "STUDY", KAPPA_ARM = "ARM")))
# "Another pairing gives no drop": studies 1-4, 2-5 and 3-6 under one sponsor each.
other_pairing <- arm_data |> mutate(ID = c(1, 2, 3, 1, 2, 3)[STUDY], ARM = OCC) |> arrange(ID, STUDY)
fit_other <- ferx_fit(sponsor_model, other_pairing, verbose = FALSE)
stopifnot(fit_other$converged, abs(fit$ofv - fit_other$ofv) < 1,
          fit_other$omega[1, 1] < 0.01 * fit_sponsor$omega[1, 1])
# Nested levels: FOCE and FOCEI only.
nested_method_codes <- sapply(c("saem", "imp", "laplace"), function(m) tryCatch({
  suppressWarnings(ferx_fit(sponsor_model, nested_data, method = m, settings = list(maxiter = 0), verbose = FALSE)); "fitted"
}, error = function(e) e$code))
stopifnot(all(nested_method_codes == "E_NESTED_LEVEL_METHOD_UNSUPPORTED"))
```

With no sponsor effect, the levelled model is the bundled model under another layout: the same objective, a study kappa equal to `ETA_E0`, the same arm γ² and the same placebo levels. One level below the subject is what `iov_column` already declared.

Adding `ETA_SP` lowers the OFV by `r round(fit$ofv - fit_sponsor$ofv, 1)` for one more parameter, and the sponsor variance (`r signif(fit_sponsor$omega[1, 1], 3)`) takes all of the between-study variance. The study kappa collapses to `r signif(fit_sponsor$omega_iov[1, 1], 1)`, with a shrinkage of `r sprintf("%.1f", 100 * fit_sponsor$shrinkage_kappa[["K_ST"]])`%, on the optimizer's lower guard, and ferx says so with a `parameter_at_runaway_guard` warning. That is not evidence for a sponsor effect. The generator has none, and three sponsors are too few to estimate a variance: the drop is what this particular pairing of six study effects happens to give. Pairing studies 1-4, 2-5 and 3-6 instead gives no drop at all (an OFV difference of `r sprintf("%.3f", abs(fit$ofv - fit_other$ofv))`), with a sponsor variance of `r signif(fit_other$omega[1, 1], 1)`. With real sponsors, judge such a split on more groups than this.

A variance on the guard has almost no curvature, so a standard error for it would mean nothing. ferx reports none and lists the variance in `fit$held_at_bound`. When the covariance step's matrix is clean, as here, it also holds the variance as it holds a `FIX` parameter:

```{r}
#| label: nested-held
fit_sponsor$held_at_bound
fit_sponsor$estimates[c("ETA_SP", "K_ST", "KAPPA_ARM"), c("estimate", "se", "rse_pct")]
fit_sponsor[c("converged", "status_label", "status_reasons", "covariance_status")]
```

```{r}
#| label: check-nested-held
#| include: false
# The prose: K_ST is the one held parameter, a kappa collapsed at the guard; its SE is NA in
# estimates and N/A in print, while fit$se_kappa holds 0, as fit$se_sigma does for the FIX sigma; every
# other estimated parameter keeps its SE; the covariance step ran; the status is CONVERGED with
# no reasons (a held collapse is not a reason). Under the second pairing the held
# parameter is ETA_SP. The levelled fit without a sponsor effect holds nothing.
held_sponsor <- fit_sponsor$held_at_bound
sponsor_print <- capture.output(print(fit_sponsor))
stopifnot(nrow(held_sponsor) == 1, identical(held_sponsor$parameter, "K_ST"), identical(held_sponsor$kind, "kappa"),
          identical(held_sponsor$reason, "collapsed_at_guard"),
          is.na(fit_sponsor$estimates["K_ST", "se"]), is.na(fit_sponsor$estimates["K_ST", "rse_pct"]),
          with(fit_sponsor$estimates, !anyNA(se[!fixed & param != "K_ST"])),
          isTRUE(fit_sponsor$estimates["ADD_ERR", "fixed"]), is.na(fit_sponsor$estimates["ADD_ERR", "se"]),
          all(fit_sponsor$se_sigma == 0),
          any(grepl("K_ST at STUDY.*SE = N/A", sponsor_print)),
          identical(unname(fit_sponsor$se_kappa["K_ST"]), 0),
          fit_sponsor$covariance_status == "computed",
          isTRUE(fit_sponsor$converged), identical(fit_sponsor$status, "converged"),
          identical(fit_sponsor$status_label, "CONVERGED"), length(fit_sponsor$status_reasons) == 0,
          identical(fit_other$held_at_bound$parameter, "ETA_SP"), identical(fit_other$held_at_bound$kind, "omega"),
          identical(fit_other$held_at_bound$reason, "collapsed_at_guard"),
          nrow(fit_levels$held_at_bound) == 0)
# The cost sentence: the widest inner problem, one eta plus a kappa per study and per arm of a sponsor.
inner_width <- nested_data |> group_by(ID) |>
  summarise(width = 1 + n_distinct(STUDY) + n_distinct(paste(STUDY, ARM))) |> pull(width)
stopifnot(sum(inner_width) == fit_sponsor$n_subjects + sum(sapply(fit_sponsor$ebe_kappas_by_level, nrow)))
```

`K_ST` is listed with the reason `collapsed_at_guard`. Its standard error is `NA` in `fit$estimates`, and the print shows `SE = N/A` on its line (below); every other estimated parameter keeps its own, from a covariance step conditional on the held variance. `fit$se_kappa` holds the engine's `r unname(fit_sponsor$se_kappa["K_ST"])` for it, as it would for a `FIX` parameter, so take the standard error from `fit$estimates`. Under the second pairing the held parameter is the sponsor variance `ETA_SP` instead.

The verdict of this fit is still `r fit_sponsor$status_label`, with no reasons. A collapse the covariance step holds does not lower the status; one it could not hold would appear in `fit$status_reasons` as `collapsed_at_guard: K_ST`. So neither `converged` nor `status` tells you that this model has one variance fewer than it declares. `fit$held_at_bound` does, with the warning.

A coarse `ID` costs more per fit. A subject's random effects are solved together, its eta and one kappa per group of every level inside it, so with the sponsor as `ID` the largest inner problem here has `r max(inner_width)` of them. Make `ID` the coarsest grouping that needs its own random effect, and declare a level only where its kappa is needed; ferx-core [measures how the cost grows](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/iov.html#nested-levels-cost).

The print labels each kappa with its level, and each level's estimates are returned once per group:

```{r}
#| label: nested-output
grep(" at (STUDY|ARM)", capture.output(print(fit_sponsor)), value = TRUE)
fit_sponsor$kappa_levels
sapply(fit_sponsor$ebe_kappas_by_level, nrow)
head(fit_sponsor$ebe_kappas_by_level$STUDY)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-nested-output
#| include: false
# The prose: one row per study (6) and per arm (22), where ebe_kappas repeats the study kappa on each arm.
stopifnot(identical(sapply(fit_sponsor$ebe_kappas_by_level, nrow), c(STUDY = 6L, ARM = 22L)),
          nrow(distinct(nested_data, STUDY, ARM)) == 22)
```

`fit$kappa_levels` names each kappa's level, and `fit$ebe_kappas_by_level` has one data frame per level: each study's `K_ST` once (`r nrow(fit_sponsor$ebe_kappas_by_level$STUDY)` rows) and each arm's `KAPPA_ARM` once (`r nrow(fit_sponsor$ebe_kappas_by_level$ARM)` rows), with the labels that identify the group. The shrinkage of a kappa and its typical weight are taken over the groups of its own level. Nested levels are estimated by FOCE and FOCEI only, and other methods are refused; see [nested levels](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/iov.html#nested-levels) in ferx-core.

### A correlation line on nested levels

The bundled `nested_levels` example has a nested design of its own: 12 sponsors, each with two studies of two arms, and five visits per arm. It has a random effect at every level, a sponsor `ETA_SP`, a study kappa `K_ST` and an arm kappa `K_ARM` weighted by arm size:

```{r}
#| label: nested-example
nested <- ferx_example("nested_levels")
invisible(ferx_model_get_section(nested$model, "parameters"))
fit_nested <- ferx_fit(nested$model, nested$data, verbose = FALSE)
c(converged = fit_nested$converged, ofv = fit_nested$ofv)
```

On a model with nested levels, the `by` of a `correlation` line may name a level. `by ARM` then groups the rows by that level's groups, nested by key, so arm 1 of study 1 and arm 1 of study 2 are two groups, as they are two arms:

```{r}
#| label: nested-correlation
nested_correlation <- function(by, file) {
  lines <- readLines(nested$model)
  lines <- sub("  sigma ADD ~ 0.25", "  theta RHO(0.3, 0.0, 0.95)\n  sigma ADD ~ 0.25", lines, fixed = TRUE)
  lines <- sub("DV ~ additive(ADD)", sprintf("DV ~ additive(ADD)\n  correlation car1(RHO) by %s", by),
               lines, fixed = TRUE)
  stopifnot(sum(grepl("RHO", lines)) == 2)
  path <- file.path(mbma_dir, file)
  writeLines(lines, path)
  path
}
fit_nested_car1 <- ferx_fit(nested_correlation("ARM", "nested_car1.ferx"), nested$data, verbose = FALSE)
c(independent = fit_nested$ofv, car1 = fit_nested_car1$ofv, rho = fit_nested_car1$theta[["RHO"]])
try(ferx_fit(nested_correlation("(STUDY, ARM)", "nested_car1_list.ferx"), nested$data, verbose = FALSE))
```

```{r}
#| label: check-nested-correlation
#| include: false
list_code <- tryCatch({
  ferx_fit(nested_correlation("(STUDY, ARM)", "nested_car1_list.ferx"), nested$data, verbose = FALSE); NULL
}, error = function(e) e$code)
# "The same cs refusal applies ... here ARM": cs by ARM beside K_ARM at ARM.
nested_cs <- sub("car1(RHO) by ARM", "cs(RHO) by ARM", readLines(nested_correlation("ARM", "nested_cs.ferx")), fixed = TRUE)
writeLines(nested_cs, file.path(mbma_dir, "nested_cs.ferx"))
nested_cs_code <- tryCatch({ ferx_fit(file.path(mbma_dir, "nested_cs.ferx"), nested$data, verbose = FALSE); NULL },
                           error = function(e) e$code)
stopifnot(isTRUE(fit_nested$converged), isTRUE(fit_nested_car1$converged), fit_nested_car1$ofv < fit_nested$ofv,
          identical(list_code, "E_RESIDUAL_CORRELATION_GROUPING_AMBIGUOUS"),
          any(grepl("cs(RHO) by ARM", nested_cs, fixed = TRUE)),
          identical(nested_cs_code, "E_RESIDUAL_CORRELATION_CONFOUNDED_KAPPA"))
```

The line lowers the OFV by `r sprintf("%.1f", fit_nested$ofv - fit_nested_car1$ofv)` at `ρ` = `r sprintf("%.2f", fit_nested_car1$theta[["RHO"]])`; as above, calibrate that drop by simulation before reading it as serial correlation. Naming a level inside a list of columns is refused, because a level already groups rows by its whole key path. The same `cs` refusal as before applies to a level that carries a kappa, here `ARM`. The ferx-core page on [residual correlation with kappa and nested levels](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/residual-correlation.html#with-kappa-and-nested-levels) lists how each form of `by` is read.

## Saving and reloading the fit

A `.fitrx` file keeps the level layout: which data columns define the block, its contrast and its levels. A reloaded fit can therefore be used for predictions, simulations, SIR and covariance without the original R session:

```{r}
#| label: fitrx
fitrx_path <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_placebo.fitrx")
ferx_save_fit(fit, fitrx_path)
fit_loaded <- ferx_load_fit(fitrx_path)
identical(fit_loaded$theta_levels, fit$theta_levels)
all.equal(fit_loaded$theta, fit$theta)
cov_loaded <- ferx_covariance(fit_loaded)
```
