```{r}
all.equal(cov_loaded$se_theta, fit$se_theta, tolerance = 1e-4)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-fitrx
#| include: false
# The prose says the reloaded covariance step agrees, not that it is bit-identical.
stopifnot(isTRUE(all.equal(cov_loaded$se_theta, fit$se_theta, tolerance = 1e-4)))
```

The covariance step on the reloaded fit gives the same standard errors as the original fit, to the tolerance shown. @sec-reproducibility covers `.fitrx` files in general.

## Uncertainty: SIR and the covariance step

`ferx_sir()` and `ferx_covariance()` run on an MBMA fit like on any other (@sec-uncertainty). They follow the fit's own settings: the inner-loop and scoring settings it was estimated with (`fit$scoring_settings`) and, for `ferx_sir()`, the SIR settings recorded in the fit (`fit$sir_settings`). Arguments you leave out are taken from the fit, not from the function's defaults. So `ferx_sir()` on a fit that already carries an SIR repeats that SIR, with the same number of draws and the same seed:

```{r}
#| label: sir
fit_sir <- ferx_sir(fit, sir_seed = 7, sir_keep_samples = TRUE)
fit_sir$sir_settings[c("samples", "resamples", "seed", "keep_samples")]
fit_sir$sir_ess
fit_sir$sir_ci_kappa
fit_sir_again <- ferx_sir(fit_sir)
c(seed = fit_sir_again$sir_seed_used, ess = fit_sir_again$sir_ess)
identical(fit_sir_again$sir_ci_theta, fit_sir$sir_ci_theta)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-sir
#| include: false
stopifnot(fit_sir_again$sir_seed_used == 7, identical(fit_sir_again$sir_ci_theta, fit_sir$sir_ci_theta))
```

With the resampled vectors kept (`sir_keep_samples = TRUE`), `ferx_sir()` also fills in each placebo level's 95% SIR interval in `theta_levels`, the derived levels included:

```{r}
#| label: sir-levels
head(fit_sir$theta_levels[, c("label", "theta_name", "value", "se", "sir_lo", "sir_hi")], 4)
```

```{r}
#| label: check-sir-levels
#| include: false
tl <- fit_sir$theta_levels
stopifnot(!anyNA(tl$sir_lo), !anyNA(tl$sir_hi[is.na(tl$theta_name)]), all(tl$sir_lo <= tl$value & tl$value <= tl$sir_hi),
          # the sentence below: the first derived level is among the four rows shown, and it is study 1's
          any(is.na(head(tl$theta_name, 4))), tl$group[which(is.na(tl$theta_name))[1]] == 0)
```

Row `r which(is.na(fit_sir$theta_levels$theta_name))[1]`, `r fit_sir$theta_levels$label[which(is.na(fit_sir$theta_levels$theta_name))[1]]`, is study 1's derived level: it has no theta of its own, so its `theta_name` is `NA` (see *The placebo levels* above), and its interval comes from the same draws as the free levels' intervals.

The effective sample size, the number of the weighted proposal draws that effectively count, depends strongly on the seed for this model. Check a few seeds before trusting one set of intervals:

```{r}
#| label: sir-seeds
sapply(c(1, 2, 7), function(s) ferx_sir(fit, sir_seed = s)$sir_ess)
```

`ferx_covariance()` likewise takes `mu_referencing` from the fit when you do not pass it. The sandwich estimator `"rsr"` gives standard errors that do not rely on the residual model being right:

```{r}
#| label: covariance
fit$scoring_settings$mu_referencing
fit_rsr <- ferx_covariance(fit, covariance_method = "rsr")
data.frame(r = fit$se_theta[1:4], rsr = fit_rsr$se_theta[1:4])
fit_s <- ferx_covariance(fit, covariance_method = "s")
fit_s$covariance_status
```

The `"s"` estimator alone fails here. It is built from the cross-product of the per-subject scores, and a meta-analysis has few subjects: `r fit$n_subjects` studies cannot determine `r fit$n_parameters` parameters. Use `"r"` or `"rsr"` for an MBMA with fewer studies than parameters. This is the other case that `converged` does not show: `fit_s$converged` is still `r fit_s$converged`, while its status is `r fit_s$status_label`, with the reason `covariance_failed`.

```{r}
#| label: check-covariance
#| include: false
stopifnot(fit_rsr$covariance_status == "computed", fit_s$covariance_status == "failed",
          isTRUE(fit_s$converged), identical(fit_s$status, "converged_with_issues"),
          identical(fit_s$status_reasons, "covariance_failed"), identical(fit_rsr$status, "converged"),
          fit$n_subjects < fit$n_parameters,
          any(grepl("rank-deficient", ferx_get_warnings(fit_s, as_df = TRUE)$message)))
```

## Pitfalls

- **Simulate and predict on the fitted cells only.** The placebo levels exist for the study-by-visit cells in the fit data. A visit or a study the fit never saw has no level, and ferx refuses it rather than assume 0:

  ```{r}
  #| label: new-visit
  new_visit <- arm_data[arm_data$STUDY == 1 & arm_data$OCC == 1, ][1, ]
  new_visit$TIME <- 6
  try(ferx_simulate(mbma$model, new_visit, n_sim = 1, fit = fit))
  ```

  To pool visits into windows, number the cells yourself with `ferx_mbma_data(index = ...)` or `levels =` and use the counted form `theta PLACEBO[N]`.
- **A standard deviation is not a standard error.** Pass a between-patient SD as `sd =` so `ferx_mbma_data()` divides it by `sqrt(n)`. `print()` shows the SD the standard errors imply; it should look like a patient-level SD.
- **The OFV includes the weights.** ferx scores on the natural scale, so the OFV differs from that of a model fitted to `DV / SE` by a term that depends only on the data. It cancels from every OFV difference between models on the same rows and weights. See the ferx-core [error model](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/error-model.html#residual-weighting-weight-...) page; its [OFV conventions across tools](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/model-file/error-model.html#ofv-conventions) table gives the constants that separate a ferx OFV from the figure NONMEM or nlmixr2 reports, for the natural-scale and the hand-built forms of the weighting.
- **`weight =` needs an additive term.** On a purely proportional error model the weight would cancel out, so ferx refuses it. A weighted kappa is likewise refused anywhere but `[individual_parameters]`, where its scaling is applied:

  ```{r}
  #| label: weight-refusals
  model_lines <- readLines(mbma$model)
  proportional_lines <- sub("DV ~ additive(ADD_ERR) weight = SE", "DV ~ proportional(ADD_ERR) weight = SE",
                            model_lines, fixed = TRUE)
  stopifnot(any(grepl("proportional(ADD_ERR) weight = SE", proportional_lines, fixed = TRUE)))
  proportional_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_proportional.ferx")
  writeLines(proportional_lines, proportional_model)
  try(ferx_fit(proportional_model, mbma$data, verbose = FALSE))
  kappa_lines <- sub("y    = BASE - DRUG", "y    = BASE - DRUG + KAPPA_ARM", model_lines, fixed = TRUE)
  stopifnot(any(grepl("BASE - DRUG + KAPPA_ARM", kappa_lines, fixed = TRUE)))
  kappa_model <- file.path(mbma_dir, "mbma_kappa_in_prediction.ferx")
  writeLines(kappa_lines, kappa_model)
  try(ferx_fit(kappa_model, mbma$data, verbose = FALSE))
  ```
- **One start may not be the best optimum.** A small arm-level model can have more than one optimum, and a fit of arm-level data is quick, so repeating it from several perturbed starts with `n_starts` (@sec-estimation-methods) is a cheap check:

  ```{r}
  #| label: multistart
  fit_multi <- ferx_fit(mbma$model, mbma$data, settings = list(n_starts = 8), verbose = FALSE)
  c(single = fit$ofv, multi = fit_multi$ofv)
  fit_multi$status_label
  ```

  ```{r}
  #| label: check-multistart
  #| include: false
  # The prose: eight starts ran, and gave the same OFV to the digits printed and the same estimates.
  stopifnot(fit_multi$n_starts == 8, identical(fit_multi$status, "converged"),
            abs(fit_multi$ofv - fit$ofv) < 5e-6,
            isTRUE(all.equal(fit_multi$theta, fit$theta, tolerance = 1e-3)),
            abs(fit_multi$omega[1, 1] / fit$omega[1, 1] - 1) < 1e-3,
            abs(fit_multi$omega_iov[1, 1] / fit$omega_iov[1, 1] - 1) < 1e-3)
  multi_note <- "multi_start" %in% ferx_get_warnings(fit_multi, as_df = TRUE)$category
  ```

  On `mbma_placebo` the eight starts find nothing better: the same OFV and the same estimates as the single start. A fit whose best start is not the first carries an info note in the `multi_start` category. `r if (multi_note) "This one does, and the equal OFVs show that the note alone does not mean a better optimum: which start comes out lowest by a margin below the printed precision can differ from one machine to the next." else "This one has none: the first start won."` Compare the OFV with the single-start fit, not the note. This result is for this model and these data; ferx-core's [multi-start on small datasets](https://ferx-nlme.org/ferx-core/examples/multistart.html#small-datasets) cites a report of arm-level models on which other starts did reach a better optimum.

### Warnings you may see here

No warning category has this chapter as its home. The fits above raise these, which other chapters explain:

- `inflated_rse` (@sec-diagnostics), because some placebo levels are small relative to their standard errors, which is expected for an unstructured placebo time course;
- the `threads` note (@sec-estimation-methods), on a machine with more cores than the subjects (six studies, three sponsors in the nested fits);
- `boundary_estimate` (@sec-diagnostics), on the profiled level held on its bound;
- `dw_autocorrelation` (@sec-diagnostics), on the first fit (Durbin-Watson `r round(fit$dw_statistic, 2)`: its residuals read as negatively autocorrelated) and on the fits that share its model and data: the fit of the arm table, the multi-start fit, the `car1` fits, the study- and sponsor-level fits, and the SIR and covariance re-runs. The fixed-study fits, the responder and proportion fits and the `nested_levels` fits (Durbin-Watson `r round(fit_nested$dw_statistic, 2)`) do not raise it;
- `parameter_at_runaway_guard` (@sec-estimation-methods), on a variance that collapses to zero: the study kappa beside the sponsor effect, and the sponsor effect itself under the second pairing, which also raises `eta_shrinkage` (@sec-diagnostics);
- `covariance_failed` and `covariance_step` (@sec-uncertainty), from the `"s"` and `"rsr"` covariance steps;
- `multi_start` (@sec-estimation-methods), an info note on the multi-start fit when a start other than the first wins.

A profiled fit can also carry a `gradient_fallback` note (@sec-estimation-methods), `W_PROFILE_FD_GRADIENT`: a subject's profiled levels got a finite-difference gradient instead of the exact one, which is correct but slower. None of the profiled fits in this chapter needs it.

```{r}
#| label: check-warning-list
#| include: false
# The list above: every category the chapter's fits raise is named there, and each named one occurs.
# threads and multi_start depend on the machine (core count; which start wins a tie), so they may be absent.
# gradient_fallback (W_PROFILE_FD_GRADIENT) is not listed, so this also backs "None of the profiled
# fits ... needs it" for every profiled fit, fit_unbounded included.
chapter_fits <- list(fit, fit_table, fit_fixed, fit_profiled, profiled_s, profiled_rsr, fit_tight, fit_unbounded, fit_car1,
                     fit_car1_profiled, fit_resp, fit_resp_profiled, fit_probit, fit_probit_profiled, fit_prop, fit_prop_profiled, fit_levels, fit_sponsor, fit_other, fit_nested, fit_nested_car1, fit_sir, fit_rsr, fit_s, fit_multi)
chapter_categories <- unique(unlist(lapply(chapter_fits, function(f) ferx_get_warnings(f, as_df = TRUE)$category)))
listed <- c("inflated_rse", "threads", "boundary_estimate", "dw_autocorrelation", "parameter_at_runaway_guard", "eta_shrinkage", "covariance_failed", "covariance_step", "multi_start")
other_categories <- ferx_get_warnings(fit_other, as_df = TRUE)$category
stopifnot(all(chapter_categories %in% listed), all(setdiff(listed, c("threads", "multi_start")) %in% chapter_categories),
          all(c("parameter_at_runaway_guard", "eta_shrinkage") %in% other_categories))
# The dw_autocorrelation item: exactly the fits it names raise it, negative (DW above 2) on the
# first fit, and fit_nested's DW is inside the thresholds.
named_fits <- list(fit = fit, fit_table = fit_table, fit_fixed = fit_fixed, fit_profiled = fit_profiled,
                   profiled_s = profiled_s, profiled_rsr = profiled_rsr, fit_tight = fit_tight,
                   fit_unbounded = fit_unbounded, fit_car1 = fit_car1, fit_car1_profiled = fit_car1_profiled,
                   fit_resp = fit_resp, fit_resp_profiled = fit_resp_profiled, fit_probit = fit_probit,
                   fit_probit_profiled = fit_probit_profiled, fit_prop = fit_prop, fit_prop_profiled = fit_prop_profiled,
                   fit_levels = fit_levels, fit_sponsor = fit_sponsor, fit_other = fit_other, fit_nested = fit_nested,
                   fit_nested_car1 = fit_nested_car1, fit_sir = fit_sir, fit_rsr = fit_rsr, fit_s = fit_s,
                   fit_multi = fit_multi)
stopifnot(length(named_fits) == length(chapter_fits))
has_dw <- vapply(named_fits, function(f) "dw_autocorrelation" %in% ferx_get_warnings(f, as_df = TRUE)$category, logical(1))
stopifnot(setequal(names(has_dw)[has_dw], c("fit", "fit_table", "fit_car1", "fit_car1_profiled", "fit_levels",
                                            "fit_sponsor", "fit_other", "fit_sir", "fit_rsr", "fit_s", "fit_multi")),
          fit$dw_statistic > 2.5, fit_nested$dw_statistic < 2.5, fit_nested$dw_statistic > 1.5)
```

## Summary

- Arm-level data have one row per study, arm and visit; `ferx_mbma_data()` builds and checks that layout from a published table.
- `DV ~ additive(ADD_ERR) weight = SE` with `ADD_ERR` fixed at 1 is inverse-variance weighting on the natural scale.
- `kappa ... weight = NARM` is between-arm variability that shrinks with arm size. Report the unweighted γ² and the effective SD at the typical arm, `sqrt(gamma2 / fit$kappa_weight_typical)`.
- With `contrast = sum_to_zero_within`, `TVE0` is each study's mean placebo level over its visits, not its week-0 level.
- An observed proportion with its standard error is a bounded continuous endpoint: `y = pnorm(LP)` (probit) or `y = inv_logit(LP)` (logit) keeps the prediction in (0, 1).
- A level block read linearly, inside one logit or probit link that is the whole prediction, or by a `[binary_model]` logit or probit predictor, as for a responder endpoint, can be declared `profile`: the levels are solved at every step instead of searched, with the same objective, and estimates within a small fraction of their standard errors. Its bounds still apply, and a level held on one is listed in `fit$held_at_bound` (the older `fit$profiled_levels_at_bound` is deprecated).
- `correlation car1(RHO) by OCC` correlates an arm's visits beside the arm kappa (`cs` there is refused). With few studies, calibrate its likelihood-ratio test by simulation.
- `fit$theta_levels` holds every placebo level's value and standard error, derived ones included, and its SIR interval after `ferx_sir(sir_keep_samples = TRUE)`. Large blocks print as one THETA BLOCKS line.
- `level NAME by COLUMN in PARENT` declares nested groupings below the subject, such as sponsor, study and arm, and `kappa ... at LEVEL` draws a kappa once per group of a level.
- `ferx_contrast_vpc()` checks the model on the treatment contrast within a study, where the between-study variability cancels.
- `.fitrx` files keep the level layout, and `ferx_sir()` and `ferx_covariance()` follow the fit's settings.
- Read `fit$status` and `fit$held_at_bound`, not `fit$converged` alone: a failed covariance step lowers the status, and a variance collapsed onto the guard is listed as held, with no standard error. On arm-level data, `n_starts = 8` is a cheap check on the optimum.

Next: @sec-experimental covers experimental model features.
